letter.title: Understanding Evergreen Alternative Funds
paragraphs: You may have come across the term "evergreen" alternative fund. This letter explains what that means, how these vehicles work, and how they differ from the closed-end private funds many of you already know from private equity and real estate investing.

A traditional closed-end private fund raises money once, invests it over a set period, and returns capital as investments are sold, typically over many years. There is no ability to add or withdraw along the way. An evergreen fund is structured differently. It has no fixed end date, and it offers periodic windows, often monthly or quarterly, when investors can subscribe new capital or request redemptions.

That periodic liquidity is a feature, not a guarantee. Each fund sets its own limits on how much can be redeemed at any given window, often expressed as a portion of the fund's assets. In periods of heavy redemption requests, a fund can prorate or delay withdrawals until the next window. Investors should think of this as liquidity that is more frequent than a closed-end fund, but still constrained and not comparable to a public market where shares trade daily without limit.

Because evergreen funds hold private, less liquid assets, such as private credit, private equity positions, or real estate, the fund's ability to meet redemption requests depends on cash on hand, new subscriptions coming in, and the manager's ability to sell assets when needed. This structural tension between periodic liquidity and underlying illiquid holdings is the central risk to understand. Valuations are also typically set periodically rather than continuously, which means the price used for a subscription or redemption may not reflect real-time market conditions.

Evergreen funds can offer a different way to gain exposure to private markets, with more flexibility around entry and exit timing than a traditional closed-end structure. They cannot offer daily liquidity, and they do not eliminate the underlying illiquidity or valuation uncertainty of the assets they hold.

We are sharing this as background, not as a recommendation. Whether a structure like this fits your broader portfolio depends on your goals, time horizon, and liquidity needs. We would welcome the chance to discuss this with you directly.

talking_points: Evergreen funds have no fixed end date and offer periodic subscription and redemption windows, unlike closed-end funds that lock up capital for a set term.
Redemptions are typically capped at each window, so a client asking to withdraw is not guaranteed to get the full amount back immediately.
Client question: "Can I get my money out whenever I want?" Answer: No. Redemptions happen only at set intervals and are subject to fund-imposed limits.

Client question: "Is this the same as a public mutual fund?" Answer: No. The underlying holdings are private and less liquid, even though the fund offers more frequent access than a traditional closed-end private fund.
Valuations in these funds are usually set periodically rather than continuously, so the price at a given window may lag real-time conditions.
The core risk to explain is the mismatch between periodic liquidity offered to investors and the illiquid nature of the assets the fund actually holds.

Client question: "Does this replace our private equity or real estate holdings?" Answer: This letter is educational only. Whether any structure fits depends on individual circumstances, worth discussing directly.
Frame the conversation as background information to support a broader discussion about how private market exposure fits into the client's overall plan.
Marchetti Ruiz Family Advisors.tailoring: Given this firm's existing allocations to private equity and real estate, the letter frames evergreen structures specifically in contrast to the closed-end funds these clients already know.

letter.title: Understanding Evergreen Alternative Funds
paragraphs: You may have heard the term evergreen fund used alongside more familiar private investments. This note explains what that means and how these structures differ from the private funds many of you already hold.

Traditional closed-end private funds raise money once, invest it over several years, and return capital as investments are sold. Your money is generally locked up for the life of the fund, often a decade or more, with no ability to add or withdraw along the way.

Evergreen funds work differently. They are designed to stay open indefinitely rather than wind down on a set schedule. Instead of a single closing, they accept new investment at regular intervals, and they offer periodic opportunities for investors to request withdrawals, commonly monthly or quarterly.

That periodic liquidity is a feature, not a guarantee. Each fund sets its own limits on how much can be redeemed at any one interval, often a modest percentage of the fund's assets. If redemption requests are heavy, the fund can prorate or delay them. These limits exist because the fund's underlying investments are longer-term and less liquid by design, and the fund needs a way to manage withdrawal requests without having to sell those holdings on a set timetable.

Because of this structure, evergreen funds can invest in the same kinds of assets as traditional private funds, such as private businesses, real assets, or private credit, while offering more flexibility around timing than a fully locked-up structure. They do not offer the same liquidity as public markets, and they are not a substitute for cash reserves or short-term savings.

The main risks are similar in kind to other private investments: the underlying assets can be difficult to value precisely, liquidity is conditional rather than assured, and fees and structures vary meaningfully from one fund to another. Reading the specific terms of any fund matters more than the general category it falls into.

We are not recommending a specific allocation through this note. If you would like to talk through whether this type of structure fits your broader plan, your advisor is glad to walk through it with you.

talking_points: Evergreen funds stay open on an ongoing basis rather than closing after one fundraising period.
They offer periodic windows, often monthly or quarterly, where investors can request withdrawals, unlike traditional funds that lock up capital for years.
Client question: Can I get my money out whenever I want? Answer: No. Withdrawals happen at set intervals and the fund can limit or delay them if requests are heavy.
Client question: Are these safer than regular private funds? Answer: Not safer, just structured for more flexibility. The underlying investments carry similar risks.
The periodic liquidity limits exist because the fund's holdings are longer-term and less liquid, so the fund manages withdrawals within that reality rather than promising immediate access.

Client question: Does this replace the closed-end private equity I already own? Answer: Not necessarily. It is a different structure that can hold similar types of assets, and whether it fits depends on your specific situation.
Fees, terms, and redemption limits vary by fund, so the details of any specific fund matter more than the general category.
This is background information only. Your advisor can go over whether this structure has a place in your plan.
